story_text.value:
Hello.

This is a follow-up to the post https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50317548

I've got tons of feedback. Thank you all so much for that!

The main issue was an absence of tutorial. I've added it. Hope it helps.

Since many people have played, I've noticed that many people start the game, but almost no one finishes it. Is the game hard? What is the main obstacle?

Most people, when see opened HA......, try to enter the word that start with HA and give up, forgetting that the first letter can be B as well. It is not necessary to enter specific words. You can submit whatever word you like.

So, I'd like to ask for your advice. How to improve the game, so that more people finish it? Maybe I shouldn't make it a daily game with increasing difficulty throughout the week? The same board hides multiple words. I thought that some sort of a challenge would be a good idea, but don't know how to implement it: https://www.jointter.com/2026-11-02/?w=PUP

The idea of the game is good, but mechanics and gameplay are far from perfect.

As before, constructive criticism is always welcome.

You can test and retest the game at https://www.jointter.com

Thank you very much!

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I'm Leon. Thrum runs the coding agents you already use as one team, on your own machine.

What it does differently from other agent orchestrators: - It is runtime agnostic. It runs Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, Copilot, Muse and Antigravity, and you can mix them: the implementer on one model, the reviewer on another. - You talk to one coordinator. It creates and directs the other agents, in all of your other projects. They message each other and check each other's work, and every message is a record you can read. The coordinator is your central point of contact for all your projects. - A stuck permission prompt reaches your phone. Reply y or n to the Telegram notice, and Thrum answers the prompt in that agent's pane. - It's a program next to your Git repo, using your own AI accounts and tokens. Nothing hosted sits between you and your AI provider. - It has extended agent memory, state and a queue for the agents to use to keep track of what they are doing. - You can search the whole history of your agents' conversations or ask your coordinator to do a full semantic search across those same conversations

I use thrum to build thrum every day building multiple features simultaneously, day in and day out, through the coordinator. The Thrum repo went from about 15 agents in april to over 100, across eight machines, with almost 700,000 messages. Thrum can scale!

The story: https://thrum.team/blog/launching-thrum-pro.html Give it a try-for free. Https://thrum.team Happy to answer any questions you have here.

story_text.value:
Native Wayland for Tk was proposed years ago as a hard GSoC project ( https://wiki.tcl-lang.org/page/GSoC+Idea%3A+Tk+Backend+for+t... ) - and let's be honest, it's very hard for humans. Turns out AI cracks it in a few hours.

Claude was given the freedom to make its choices from top to bottom, including stack and architecture. It came up with a thin X11 emulation layer, the same approach Tk's macOS and Windows ports already take - except this one is shared by Wayland and Android thanks to their similarity. The human in the loop merely tested and sanity-checked the outcome to her unexpected satisfaction. Tkabber (a large, long-lived XMPP client) runs on the Wayland port unaltered, and on Android with one small fix.

Unlike AndroWish (an SDL-based Tcl/Tk distribution for Android), this is a backend inside Tk itself, shared with the Wayland port: Cairo/HarfBuzz drawing, with touch and the on-screen keyboard handled in generic Tk through new commands and events.

If you want to experience an anachronism, you can try the APK of the Tk demo with an added multitouch example ( https://github.com/pounceandmiss/tk-wayland/releases/ ), and full-on Tkabber on Android ( https://github.com/pounceandmiss/tkabber-demo/releases/ ).

story_text.value:
hi, i made this mostly as a joke. it started when i found that replacing (almost) all skip(';') in tcc with if(tok==';') skip(';') essentially adds some highly basic auto semicolon insertion. then i expanded on the idea and kept adding more stuff and fixing up the semicolon stuff a bit and added python style indentation.

so now it's a fork of tcc (fabrice bellard's tiny c compiler) where semicolons are optional and you can use indentation instead of braces, so you can write stuff like

    int main():
        printf("hello\n")
        return 0
its not just at the end of lines by the way

    int a, b float c // a semicolon is inserted between b and float
    for (int i=1 i <= 5 i++): // ... or between statements
        printf("%d ", i)
the indentation part is just a pass before lexing that turns lines ending in "):" or "else:" into "{" and adds the closing "}" when the indentation drops.

the obvious problem is that without semicolons a statement just keeps going as long as the next token can continue it. so if a line starts with *, ( or - it gets glued onto the previous line, same as js asi. "b = a" followed by a line with "-1" compiles fine and gives you b = a - 1. i listed the ones i know about in the readme.

normal c with semicolons still works and you can mix both. -run and shebangs work like in tcc. it can compile itself

demo page with a few examples: https://tanjim.org/slcc/demo.html

please don't use this for anything real

story_text.value:
Hey, hackers!

After failing to effectively order groceries at a local store with my Hermes assistant, I got an idea of making an all-inclusive interface to access online services.

It's a sidecar to an online service backend, a bit more compared to "just exposing the API".

Out of the box: discovery, registration, memory-hard proof-of-work to repell scrapers, payments, server-sent events, prototype KYC integration.

I've built a few demos that you can try. Links and prompts to use are on the landing page.

The reference implementation is in Ruby on Rails, something I know well. But there's nothing preventing from implementing the same for another platform.

Honest disclosure: it is initially vibe-coded, but I've manually reviewed almost every part of it.

Eager to know what you think about.

story_text.value:
Hey all, a little while ago I set up Openpanel in some of my projects but very quickly hit the limits and was starting to have to pay $50 to keep the events flowing in. I thought this was crazy, as I really wasnt sending that many events.

I was thinking, surely it can't be that expensive to store events. I looked into self hosting Openpanel, and it's even crazier. You need redis, clickhouse, postgres, beefy machine. I realized I am paying a tonne of money for features that are completely irrelevent now. I don't need instant charts. In fact, I would prefer to never even go to your ugly dashboard and figure out how to use it. So i'm paying this extreme premium so these services can compute all these indexes and what not so they can deliver me any chart I want in a second. It's crazy.

I thought about what I really needed as a lot of my work is done with claude/codex now and realized all I really wanted was to get the raw events and have my agent analyze them with duckdb, let me ask questions, and make charts.

I looked at a few ways of doing this but the simplest and cheapest was cloudflare. Literally, just store the events in R2, and then the agent can pull them down when it wants.

What I do instead is I have a 1tb SSD, I pull down my events from r2 when I want and load it into duckdb. Now my agent can do whatever it wants. It's not limited by the capabilities gifted to me by amplitude etc. Heck, it can even write python scripts or anything. You could create Jupyter notebooks to view it, so many options.

I have been using this in prod, but thought i'd open it up if anyone wants to try: https://slurp.run/

It's fully open source, and you can one click to install it. Lmk if you try it and run into any issues.

One cool thing I got working too, is you can literally point your segment/sentry clients at the cloudflare endpoint.

title.value: Show HN: Product Analytics for your agent. 100x+ cheaper analytics/BI

story_text.value:
I have been building this simulator for fun as a side project to help myself and others visualize electromagentic phenomena such as radiation, interference, coupling, polarization and diffraction. Sort of a sandbox to explore electromagnetism.

The simulator runs omn the browser and lets you: place multiple, diffrent radiation sources and set their parameters (geometery, amplitude, phase and more)

place perefect wire conductors, PEC plane and poke slots in the plane to create diffraction patterns

observe the electric field, magnetic field, energy flow field, energy density or radiation pattern

zoom in and out and translate the canvas

*change the simulation resolution, frequency and propogation speed and some other parameters

I hope someone might find it useful and I’d love to hear what people think :)

Live: https://www.antennasim.com/ GitHub: https://github.com/rotemTsafrir/antenna_sim

story_text.value:
I built the first version of this stuff a decade ago as ethanolus (c2h5oh). And I've used it for most of my projects as a backend layer since then.

The main motive is to eliminate unnecessary complexity from backend layers.

How it works: a rust nginx module calls postgresql functions via non-blocking libpq io. There is an optional patch for libpq. It provides zero-copy for nginx-chained memory buffers - to avoid request body copies between nginx and libpq.

Pgxio supports http2 and websockets. Realtime listen/notify updates from postgres without polling.

How to try - code on github. Tested on Debian - FreeBSD validation in progress.

It's alpha - so any feedback is welcome.

story_text.value:
Over the years I've tried dozens of time tracking and invoicing apps, and Harvest was the only one I liked. Primarily due to its relatively intuitive UI/UX.

I was happy to pay them a reasonable sum for the product they provide, but after the 10x price jack, I had no choice but to seek alternatives. I tried a bunch of them again, found nothing I liked.

So, with 20+ years of software engineering experience under my belt, I decided to build my own.

Here's the result: https://hourbun.com/

I first and foremost built it for my own use, then over the past week or two added features that others might need (such as approvals, quotes, expenses, etc).

I spent a lot of time making sure the UI/UX is top-notch, and the performance is even better than Harvest - the app should feel very snappy (it's hosted in the US, and I'm based in Australia, and it's still very fast for me).

If you're looking for a decent time tracking and invoicing app, give mine a try? It comes with a 14-day trial and doesn't need card details.

And in case you're wondering, no, it's not vibe-coded. AI agents were definitely a big part of building it, but the product was built with experience and care. Love to hear your thoughts and feedback.

story_text.value:
I built a browser ball-sort puzzler where levels are ordered by difficulty, starting from the easiest.

I experimented with several alternative modes with the aim to have similar complexity in other environments. Each mode has its own restrictions, which gives additional challenge for each user to find its favorite mode.

Features:

- 10 different game modes; over 1000 levels combined

- near-win finish — preemptively calculates win conditions to skip redundant endgame moves

- dynamic hints about hardest and easiest color - very helpful on hard modes

- hints — ask for the next correct move when a puzzle is too hard

- undo, restart, per-puzzle progress saved in your browser

- customize shape and styling of balls

- dark/light theme

- Offline friendly; no registration, no ads
